problems.stem: You use the same strong password for your school portal, email, and a shopping site. The shopping site reports a data breach. What is the real risk?
options: No risk, because the password was strong.
Attackers can try that leaked password on your email and school portal too, so reused passwords expose every linked account.
Only the shopping account is ever at risk in a breach.
The password becomes safe again after you log in once.
problems.explanation: A breach on one site exposes every account that reuses the password. Strength does not help once the password is leaked; uniqueness does.

problems.stem: The school portal offers two-factor authentication but it adds a code step at login. Why is turning it on worth the extra step?
options: It makes your password longer automatically.
Even if your password leaks, an attacker still cannot log in without the second factor, which blocks most takeovers.
It removes the need to remember a password.
It only matters for staff accounts, not students.
problems.explanation: Two-factor authentication blocks essentially all automated takeover attempts and the large majority of targeted ones, because the attacker would also need the second factor, not just the password.

problems.stem: You want an AI tool to help reword a complaint email. The draft contains your student ID and a classmate's full name and phone number. What should you do before pasting it in?
options: Paste the whole email; AI tools keep everything private.
Remove your student ID and the classmate's name and number first, then paste only the text you need reworded.
Paste it but ask the AI to keep it secret.
Add even more detail so the AI understands the situation.
problems.explanation: Redact identifiers and other people's private data before using an AI tool. Share only what is needed for the task. Retention also depends on the tool: consumer chatbots may keep and train on pasted text unless you opt out, while school-provided education or enterprise tiers typically do not train on input by default, so prefer the managed tool for anything sensitive.

problems.stem: You get a text: "URGENT: your student account will be locked in 1 hour. Verify now: bit.ly/uni-verify." What is the safest response?
options: Click the link quickly so the account is not locked.
Do not click; open the school portal directly through its known address and check your account there.
Reply with your password so they can confirm it is you.
Forward the link to classmates so they verify too.
problems.explanation: Urgency and shortened links are phishing signals. Never click; reach the real site directly and verify there.
